planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this variety does not come true from seed, so division of rooted rhizome sections is the standard way to propagate it. Once settled it spreads on its own and rarely needs replanting.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, including the dry, root-filled ground beneath mature trees where few other evergreens thrive; wood spurge forms low rosettes of leathery, dark-green leaves on creeping underground rhizomes, and in mid-spring each rosette sends up a stem topped with a dome of long-lasting, acid-yellow-green bracts that light up shaded corners for six weeks or more before fading to green for summer. It spreads steadily by rhizomes to knit together a dense, weed-smothering evergreen carpet, and tolerates dry shade, root competition, and neglect better than almost any other flowering groundcover, making it a workhorse under hedges, shrub borders, and shade trees. Wear gloves when dividing or cutting it back, since the milky latex sap is a skin and eye irritant common to all euphorbias; site it away from paths where bare skin might brush against broken stems. Deer and rabbits leave it alone. Shear off flowering stems after bloom to keep growth tidy and prevent excessive self-seeding of the straight species where it may be nearby.

planting.note: Transplant rhizome sections in early spring before fronds unfurl, into ordinary, even poor or sandy, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; bracken fern is almost never grown from spores in cultivation and instead is established from divided rhizome pieces taken from an existing stand. Choose the planting site with care — it will fill the space it is given and then keep going.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in ordinary, well-drained soil, even poor sand or dry clay, in partial to full shade beneath pines or hardwoods; bracken fern is one of the toughest, most drought-tolerant large ferns available, producing broad, triangular, deeply cut deciduous fronds on wiry stalks that die back to the ground each winter and re-emerge reliably each spring. It spreads by deep, far-traveling rhizomes into extensive colonies, making it excellent for stabilizing shaded slopes and covering large difficult areas where nothing else will grow, but a poor choice for small beds or anywhere it needs to stay contained — use a buried barrier or an isolated site if space is limited. Despite a long history of foraged fiddleheads, modern research has found that bracken contains compounds linked to cancer risk in both livestock and humans, so it should be treated strictly as an ornamental and erosion-control planting, not a food crop, and kept out of grazed pasture. Otherwise it is essentially maintenance-free once established, needing no fertilizer, no supplemental water beyond establishment, and no pest control.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions after the last frost into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; press the roots in firmly and keep evenly moist while the creeping stems knit together, which typically takes one full growing season for a solid mat.

directions: Plant starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, or full sun where summers are cool and soil stays consistently moist; blue star creeper forms a dense, ankle-high mat of tiny round bright-green leaves studded from late spring through summer with pale blue, five-pointed star-shaped flowers only a fraction of an inch across. It roots as it spreads, filling gaps between stepping stones and pavers and tolerating light foot traffic once established, which makes it a popular substitute for turf in small shaded paths and between patio stones. It does not tolerate drought or foot traffic as well as some steppable thymes, so keep the soil from drying out during hot weather and avoid heavy or repeated trampling. Foliage stays evergreen in mild-winter climates and dies back to the crown where winters are cold, returning reliably from the roots in spring. Trim back periodically to keep it from climbing into neighboring low plants.

planting.note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix without covering — bush violet needs light to germinate — at 70–75°F; start 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to shaded beds after all danger of frost has passed. It self-sows readily once established, so later plantings often need no help.

directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix without covering, as bush violet needs light to germinate; maintain 70–75°F soil temperature and expect germination in 2–3 weeks. Transplant after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun — this old-fashioned cottage-garden species is taller and more upright than the compact hybrid Browallia speciosa sold in bedding packs, with a looser, willowy habit topped by five-lobed violet-blue flowers with a small white eye, blooming continuously from early summer to frost. Unlike the hybrid, bush violet comes true from its own seed and self-sows readily once established, so a single planting often returns for years in beds where it is happy. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and a fuller shape, and keep soil evenly moist; it wilts visibly when dry but recovers quickly once watered. Good for cutting and for filling gaps in shaded borders through the heat of summer.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; press seeds onto the surface of the mix since they need light to germinate, then transplant out after frost danger has passed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Flowering, and therefore pyrethrin content, builds up over the plant's second and third seasons.

directions: Start seed indoors under light, since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; pyrethrum forms a low mound of finely cut, silvery-gray, aromatic foliage similar in texture to feverfew, and from late spring into summer sends up wiry stems topped with cheerful white, daisy-form flowers with yellow centers. This is the source plant of natural pyrethrin insecticide, which is concentrated in the still-closed flower heads and traditionally harvested just as the outer ring of petals opens, then dried quickly out of direct sun to preserve potency before grinding into powder. As an ornamental it needs only average care: good drainage is the one non-negotiable requirement, since wet winter soil is far more likely to kill it than cold. Plants are relatively short-lived, usually productive and vigorous for three to four years before they benefit from division or replacement. Deadhead spent flowers not being harvested to keep the plant tidy and encourage further bloom.
sources: University of Kentucky College of Agriculture
